nameStory: The Maryland golden-aster gets its name from the state where it was first scientifically described, though it actually grows throughout much of the eastern United States. The 'golden-aster' part is a bit misleading - while it looks like a classic daisy or aster with its bright yellow petals radiating from a center, it blooms much earlier than most true asters. Think of it as the golden cousin in the huge sunflower family!
description: Maryland golden-aster is a cheerful wildflower that looks like a small sunflower or bright yellow daisy. It grows as a low, somewhat sprawling plant that reaches about 1-3 feet tall and wide. The sunny yellow flowers bloom in late summer, each about an inch across with numerous thin petals surrounding a golden center. Its leaves are simple and alternate, giving the whole plant a rather soft, unpretentious appearance that belies its rarity in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow daisy-like flowers about 1 inch across, with many thin ray petals surrounding a yellow center disc. The petals feel slightly papery to the touch and the flowers often appear in loose clusters at the stem tips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Alternate, simple leaves that are lance-shaped to oval, typically 2-4 inches long. They feel slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch, with a grayish-green color that's distinctly paler than most other wildflowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a somewhat sprawling, low mound that's wider than it is tall, usually 1-3 feet in both height and spread. The stems tend to lean outward rather than growing strictly upright.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy white seed heads after flowering, similar to dandelions but smaller. Each seed has silky white bristles that help it float on the wind.

habitat: In New England, Maryland golden-aster is extremely rare and found only in sandy, well-drained soils in open areas like coastal plains, sandy fields, or disturbed sites with poor soil. It prefers full sun and seems to thrive where other plants struggle in dry, nutrient-poor conditions. Look for it in areas with other drought-tolerant wildflowers and grasses.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of grayish-green leaves. Young plants are not particularly distinctive at this stage.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow larger and begin forming flower buds in mid to late summer. The distinctive fuzzy, pale foliage becomes more noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming time is late summer into early fall, when the bright yellow flowers are unmistakable. After blooming, fluffy white seed heads develop.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving little trace above ground. Seeds may persist in the soil through winter dormancy.

funFact: Maryland golden-aster is so rare in New England that it's been documented only 3 times by naturalists - making it one of the most elusive wildflowers in the region, possibly representing the very northern edge of its natural range!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with fall-blooming goldenrods, but Maryland golden-aster has distinct daisy-like flowers with separate petals rather than goldenrod's tiny clustered flowers. The golden-aster's flowers are also much larger and more obviously daisy-shaped - think 'one big flower' versus goldenrod's 'spray of tiny flowers.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, this isn't actually native to just Maryland - the name simply reflects where botanists first formally described it. The extreme rarity in New England suggests these populations may be at the very edge of the species' comfort zone, making each sighting scientifically valuable.
compareHints: Maryland golden-aster is the only member of the Chrysopsis genus found in New England, making it unique among our golden-asters. Compared to other yellow daisy-family flowers in the region, it's distinguished by blooming later than most (late summer to fall), its particularly fuzzy grayish leaves, and its preference for very sandy, poor soils where few other flowers thrive.
